0.title: A Farewell Letter from the Rock
0.overview:
Second Peter is the apostle's last will and testament. Writing in the shadow of his own death — 'the putting off of my body will be soon, as our Lord Jesus Christ made clear to me' (1:14; cf. John 21:18–19) — Peter addresses a church under pressure from false teachers who have crept inside the community, twisted Paul's letters, and weaponized a crude uniformitarianism against the hope of Christ's return. The letter's three movements answer three threats: the erosion of moral seriousness (ch. 1: grow in the divine nature), the corruption of doctrine by immoral teachers (ch. 2: their condemnation is certain), and the mocking of eschatological hope (ch. 3: the Day is coming and it will be unlike anything the world has seen).

The letter's authorship is the most contested in the NT canon. The vocabulary differs sharply from 1 Peter, and Origen already noted that some doubted it. Eusebius placed it among the antilegomena — letters known but disputed. Yet the arguments for Petrine authorship are substantial: the self-identification is unusually specific (Simeon Peter, v.1; the eyewitness claim of vv.16–18; the reference to a prior letter in 3:1); a forger who fabricates this much personal detail is extraordinarily bold. The vocabulary difference most likely reflects a different secretary — 1 Peter was written dia Silouanou (through Silvanus, 1 Pet 5:12), while 2 Peter shows the rougher, more Semitic Greek one would expect from a Galilean fisherman writing more directly. The church ultimately recognized it as canonical, and its theological weight — the virtue chain, the transfiguration testimony, the patience of God, the new creation — fully justifies that recognition.

The relationship to Jude is unavoidable: 2 Peter 2 and Jude share extensive material (the angels, Noah, Sodom; the Balaam archetype; the waterless springs; the dog and pig proverbs). The majority of scholars believe Peter used Jude (not the reverse), which, if correct, places 2 Peter after Jude and in the mid-to-late 60s AD — consistent with Peter's death under Nero (c. 64–68 AD). Peter does not merely copy Jude; he develops, expands, and re-focuses the material for a church whose crisis has moved from external pressure to internal corruption.

1.overview:
The opening chapter lays the theological foundation for everything that follows. God's divine power has already given believers everything needed for life and godliness (v. 3) — the indicative is total and complete. From that foundation the imperative rises: make every effort, add to your faith, be diligent (vv. 5, 10). The letter opens with lavish gift and closes the chapter with urgent command — not as contradiction but as the grammar of grace. What God has fully provided, the believer is to fully pursue.

The second half of the chapter (vv. 12–21) grounds Peter's authority in two things: the apostolic eyewitness of the Transfiguration and the prophetic Scriptures. These are not two competing sources but two interlocking confirmations — history and prophecy, the visible and the written, pointing to the same Christ and the same coming Day.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–11 — Divine Power and Precious Promises
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Simeon Peter, servant and apostle, writes to those who have obtained a faith of equal standing with his by the righteousness of our God and Saviour Jesus Christ (v.1); grace and peace be multiplied in the knowledge of God (v.2). His divine power has already granted everything that pertains to life and godliness (v.3), and with it his precious and very great promises, so that through them we may become partakers of the divine nature, having escaped the world's corruption (v.4).

For this reason make every effort to supplement faith with virtue, virtue with knowledge (v.5), knowledge with self-control, self-control with steadfastness, steadfastness with godliness (v.6), godliness with brotherly affection, and that with love (v.7). If these are yours and increasing, they keep you from being ineffective in the knowledge of Christ (v.8); whoever lacks them is so nearsighted he is blind, having forgotten he was cleansed (v.9). So be diligent to confirm your calling and election, and you will never fall (v.10) — and an entrance into the eternal kingdom will be richly provided (v.11).
verseByVerse.theology:
Partakers of the Divine Nature

Verse 4 has been misread in both directions and needs stating carefully. It does not mean human beings become God or are absorbed into deity — Peter distinguishes us from him in every line, and the Creator-creature distinction is not negotiable anywhere in Scripture. What it means is participation in his moral character and his life: sharing his holiness, made alive with a life that is his. The next clause defines it negatively — 'having escaped from the corruption that is in the world' — so the divine nature shared is the opposite of corruption. It is a promise of incorruption and holiness, not of divinity.

Verse 10 has troubled readers too, and the trouble dissolves on seeing who is confirmed to whom. Peter does not say make God's election secure — that is in nobody's power, and this letter grounds everything in what divine power has granted. The establishing is in the believer's own assurance. Election is God's act and is settled; whether a man knows himself to be elect is a different question, answered by exactly these qualities appearing in his life. The fruit does not create the root; it demonstrates it — works establishing certainty, not salvation.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: 'Obtained' in verse 1 translates a word meaning to receive by lot — what falls to you rather than what you achieve. And 'of equal standing with ours' is remarkable from an eyewitness who will describe the transfiguration fifteen verses later: Peter tells readers who have seen nothing that their faith is of exactly equal value to his. There is no lesser grade for those who came after.

Now: Note that verse 3 closes a door before the false teachers can open it. If everything necessary has already been granted, no supplementary knowledge is on offer and anyone promising a further instalment is selling what does not exist. And the diagnosis in verse 9 is exact: the word for nearsighted means squinting at something close. The man is not blind to everything — he sees this week, this appetite, this grievance perfectly well; what he cannot see is anything at a distance. The root is named in the same verse: he has forgotten he was cleansed. When growth has stopped, look for a memory gone dim rather than a missing technique.

verseByVerse.quote: Simeon Peter, a servant and apostle of Jesus Christ, To those who have obtained a faith of equal standing with ours by the righteousness of our God and Savior Jesus Christ: May grace and peace be multiplied to you in the knowledge of God and of Jesus our Lord.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Simeon Peter' — and the first word is unexpected. Not Simon, the ordinary Greek form, but Simeon, the Hebrew. It appears this way only once elsewhere in the New Testament, on James's lips at the Jerusalem council (Acts 15:14).

Then both names together: the one he was born with and the one Jesus gave him. A man writing his last letter signs it with his whole history — the fisherman from Galilee and the rock.

'A servant and apostle.' Servant first — doulos, slave — and apostle second. The order is the same instinct as 1 Peter 5:1, where he called himself a fellow elder before he called himself anything else.

'To those who have obtained a faith of equal standing with ours.' The phrase is the whole letter's opening kindness, and it repays care. Obtained translates a word meaning to receive by lot — what falls to you rather than what you achieve. Faith is described as an allotment.

And 'of equal standing with ours' is remarkable coming from an eyewitness. Peter had seen the transfiguration and will describe it in fifteen verses; he tells readers who have seen nothing that their faith is of exactly equal value to his. Not a lesser grade for those who came later.

'By the righteousness of our God and Savior Jesus Christ.' In Greek this is a single article governing both nouns — the construction that identifies them as one person. Peter calls Jesus God directly, as Paul does at Titus 2:13, and it is one of the New Testament's plainest statements of his deity.

'In the knowledge of God' introduces the letter's key word. Epignosis — full knowledge — appears four times in this short letter, and it is the answer to the false teachers, who were offering knowledge of another kind.

verseByVerse.quote: His divine power has granted to us all things that pertain to life and godliness, through the knowledge of him who called us to his own glory and excellence, by which he has granted to us his precious and very great promises, so that through them you may become partakers of the divine nature, having escaped from the corruption that is in the world because of sinful desire.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'His divine power has granted to us all things that pertain to life and godliness.' Note the tense: has granted, complete. Not will supply as needed — already given, in full.

And 'all things that pertain to life and godliness' closes a door before the false teachers can open it. If everything necessary has been provided, then no supplementary knowledge is on offer, and anyone promising a further instalment is selling something that does not exist.

'Through the knowledge of him who called us to his own glory and excellence.' The channel is knowing a person, not acquiring information. And what he called us to is his own glory — not a glory he distributes but the one he possesses.

'By which he has granted to us his precious and very great promises.' Peter piles up superlatives, and 'precious' is his own recurring word — he used it of Christ the living stone and of the blood.

Then the astonishing clause: 'so that through them you may become partakers of the divine nature.'

This needs stating carefully, because it has been misread in both directions. It does not mean human beings become God, or absorb into deity — Peter has just distinguished us from him in every line. The Creator-creature distinction is not negotiable anywhere in Scripture.

What it means is participation in his moral character and his life: sharing his holiness, and being made alive with a life that is his. The next clause defines it negatively — 'having escaped from the corruption that is in the world because of sinful desire' — so the divine nature shared is the opposite of corruption. It is a promise of incorruption and holiness, not of divinity.

verseByVerse.quote: For this very reason, make every effort to supplement your faith with virtue, and virtue with knowledge, and knowledge with self-control, and self-control with steadfastness, and steadfastness with godliness, and godliness with brotherly affection, and brotherly affection with love.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'For this very reason' — because of everything just granted. The effort that follows rests on a gift already complete, which is the New Testament's invariable order.

'Make every effort to supplement your faith.' The verb behind 'supplement' is the choregos word again — the citizen who funded a chorus and paid for everything it needed, lavishly. Peter used it of God's supply; here he asks the same generosity from them. Not a grudging minimum but full provision.

Then eight qualities in a chain, each growing out of the last. And it starts where it must: faith, which is not one link among others but the ground.

Virtue is arete, moral excellence — the same word used of God in verse 3. Knowledge follows, because goodness without understanding blunders. Self-control follows knowledge, since knowing what is right settles nothing until the appetites are governed.

Steadfastness is hypomone, remaining under weight — self-control extended over time, which is a different and harder thing. Then godliness, which turns the whole sequence God-ward and prevents it becoming mere self-mastery.

And the chain ends in two words about people: brotherly affection, philadelphia, warmth toward the family; and then love, agape, which reaches past the family to everyone.

The direction is the thing to see. It runs from what God has given, through the ordering of one's own character, and out to other people — and it ends at love, which is where every such list in the New Testament ends.

verseByVerse.quote: For if these qualities are yours and are increasing, they keep you from being ineffective or unfruitful in the knowledge of our Lord Jesus Christ. For whoever lacks these qualities is so nearsighted that he is blind, having forgotten that he was cleansed from his former sins.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'For if these qualities are yours and are increasing.' Two conditions, and the second is the interesting one. Not merely present but increasing — Peter assumes growth is the normal state and that a static Christian life is already a warning sign.

'They keep you from being ineffective or unfruitful in the knowledge of our Lord Jesus Christ.' The two negatives are worth separating. Ineffective is literally idle, unemployed — the word for land lying fallow. Unfruitful is about output.

And note the sphere: ineffective in the knowledge of Christ. Peter is not saying these qualities earn knowledge, but that without them a man's knowing goes nowhere. You may hold the doctrine accurately and be entirely unproductive in it.

Then the reverse case, and the diagnosis is striking: 'whoever lacks these qualities is so nearsighted that he is blind.'

The word for nearsighted means squinting, screwing up the eyes to see something close. It is a wonderfully exact description. The man is not blind to everything — he can see what is right in front of him perfectly well: this week, this appetite, this grievance. What he cannot see is anything at a distance.

'Having forgotten that he was cleansed from his former sins.' And there is the root. He has lost sight of his own cleansing — not lost the cleansing, but the memory of it. A Christian who forgets what he was forgiven has no fuel for growth, because gratitude is the engine of the whole chain in verses 5-7.

Which suggests where to look when growth has stopped. Not usually at a missing technique, but at a memory that has gone dim.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore, brothers, be all the more diligent to confirm your calling and election, for if you practice these qualities you will never fall. For in this way there will be richly provided for you an entrance into the eternal kingdom of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Therefore, brothers, be all the more diligent to confirm your calling and election.' The sentence has troubled readers, and the trouble dissolves on a careful look at who is being confirmed to whom.

Peter does not say make God's election secure — that is not in anyone's power, and this letter grounds everything in what God's divine power has granted. The verb means to make firm, ratify, establish; and the establishing is in the believer's own assurance.

Election is God's act and is settled. Whether a man knows himself to be elect is a different question, and it is answered by exactly the qualities of verses 5-7 appearing in his life. The fruit does not create the root; it demonstrates it. That is how the Reformed tradition has always read this: not works establishing salvation, but works establishing certainty.

And there is real pastoral kindness in it. A Christian anxious about whether he is truly God's is not told to search his memory for a decisive moment, nor to look inward for a feeling. He is told to look for growth in ordinary character — which is visible, and which other people can see too.

'For if you practise these qualities you will never fall.' The word for fall is used of stumbling. It is not a promise of sinlessness but of not coming to ruin.

'For in this way there will be richly provided for you an entrance into the eternal kingdom.' The verb is the choregos word for the third time in six verses — and now the direction reverses. They were told to supply these qualities lavishly; God will lavishly supply their entrance. The generosity given comes back multiplied at the door.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 12–21 — Eyewitnesses and the Prophetic Word
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Peter intends always to remind them, though they know these things and are established in the truth (v.12), thinking it right to stir them up while he is in this tent (v.13), since he knows the putting off of his body will be soon, as Christ made clear to him (v.14) — and he will make every effort so that after his departure they may recall these things (v.15).

For they did not follow cleverly devised myths but were eyewitnesses of his majesty (v.16), when he received honour and glory from the Father and the voice came from the Majestic Glory, 'This is my beloved Son' (v.17) — a voice they themselves heard on the holy mountain (v.18). And they have the prophetic word more fully confirmed, to which the readers do well to attend as to a lamp in a dark place, until the day dawns and the morning star rises in their hearts (v.19) — knowing that no prophecy of Scripture comes from someone's own interpretation (v.20), for no prophecy was ever produced by the will of man, but men spoke from God as they were carried along by the Holy Spirit (v.21).
verseByVerse.theology:
Carried Along: How Scripture Was Given

Verse 20 is quoted in two directions and the context settles it. It is often taken to mean no individual may interpret Scripture privately — a reasonable caution, but not what Peter argues here. His subject throughout is the origin of prophecy, not its later handling, and verse 21 explains verse 20 directly, beginning with 'for'. The sense is that prophecy did not arise from the prophet's own reading of his times. It came from outside him.

Then verse 21 holds two things together, and the doctrine of Scripture lives in the combination. Men spoke — real people with their own vocabulary, style and circumstances; Isaiah does not sound like Amos. And they were carried along, which is a sailing word: it is used in Acts 27 of Paul's ship, which had lost the power to steer and was driven before the wind. The men are not passive cargo — they are working the vessel — but the direction is not theirs, and they arrive where the wind takes them. Which is why the Bible reads as both thoroughly human and entirely God's word.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: This letter is written by a man under a sentence he has carried for thirty years. Peter knows he will die soon because he was told: on the beach, after the third question about love, Jesus said that when he was old another would carry him where he did not want to go (John 21:18-19). And what he does with the knowledge is the striking thing — not settling affairs or saying farewells, but arranging for them to remember after he has gone, which is very likely why we have this letter at all.

Now: Notice what Peter selects from the transfiguration. Not the shining face, the white clothes, or Moses and Elijah — he reports the voice, because the argument concerns testimony and what settles it is not what he saw but what was said. There is restraint in it too: he had wanted to build three shelters and had spoken without knowing what he was saying, and he mentions none of that. And the lamp image in verse 19 is exactly weighted — a lamp is not the sun; it is enough to see the next few feet by, and indispensable if the alternative is total darkness. Peter is honest about how much light Scripture gives: sufficient, and not yet daylight.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore I intend always to remind you of these qualities, though you know them and are established in the truth that you have. I think it right, as long as I am in this body, to stir you up by way of reminder, since I know that the putting off of my body will be soon, as our Lord Jesus Christ made clear to me. And I will make every effort so that after my departure you may be able at any time to recall these things.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Therefore I intend always to remind you of these qualities, though you know them and are established in the truth.' Peter is not correcting ignorance. He says plainly that they know it and are established in it — and he intends to go on saying it anyway.

That is a considered view of what teaching is for, and it cuts against the appetite for novelty that the false teachers were exploiting. Most of what a congregation needs is not new information but the same truth said again, because knowing a thing and having it present to you are different states.

'To stir you up by way of reminder.' The verb means to wake someone — Peter uses it of a sleeper being roused, and he uses it again in 3:1. His model of ministry is not filling empty heads but waking drowsy ones.

'As long as I am in this body' is literally this tent, and the image governs the paragraph. A tent is temporary accommodation, struck when the journey moves on.

'Since I know that the putting off of my body will be soon, as our Lord Jesus Christ made clear to me.' Peter knows he is going to die, and he knows it because he was told. On the beach, after the third question about love, Jesus had said that when he was old another would dress him and carry him where he did not want to go — and John adds that this indicated the kind of death by which he would glorify God (John 21:18-19).

So this letter is written by a man under a sentence he has been carrying for thirty years. And what he does with the knowledge is the striking thing. 'I will make every effort so that after my departure you may be able at any time to recall these things.' He is not settling affairs or saying farewells. He is arranging for them to remember after he has gone — which is very likely why we have this letter at all.

verseByVerse.quote: For we did not follow cleverly devised myths when we made known to you the power and coming of our Lord Jesus Christ, but we were eyewitnesses of his majesty. For when he received honor and glory from God the Father, and the voice was borne to him by the Majestic Glory, "This is my beloved Son, with whom I am well pleased," we ourselves heard this very voice borne from heaven, for we were with him on the holy mountain.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'For we did not follow cleverly devised myths.' The charge is answered head-on. The false teachers were evidently saying that the promised coming of Christ was a story — and Peter's reply is not philosophical but historical.

'When we made known to you the power and coming of our Lord Jesus Christ, but we were eyewitnesses of his majesty.' The word for eyewitnesses is epoptai, and it was used in the mystery religions for those admitted to the highest grade of initiation — those who had seen. Peter takes the vocabulary of the cults his opponents traded in and applies it to something that happened on a hill in Galilee.

'For when he received honour and glory from God the Father, and the voice was borne to him by the Majestic Glory.' Peter is describing the transfiguration, and he was one of three men there.

Notice what he selects from it. He does not describe the shining face or the white clothes or Moses and Elijah. He reports the voice — 'This is my beloved Son, with whom I am well pleased' — because the argument concerns testimony, and what settles the matter is not what he saw but what was said.

'We ourselves heard this very voice borne from heaven, for we were with him on the holy mountain.' The emphasis is on hearing, twice, and on presence.

And there is something moving in the restraint. Peter had wanted to build three shelters and stay, and had spoken without knowing what he was saying. He mentions none of that. Fifty years on he reports only what is admissible: we were there, and we heard.

verseByVerse.quote: And we have the prophetic word more fully confirmed, to which you will do well to pay attention as to a lamp shining in a dark place, until the day dawns and the morning star rises in your hearts,
verseByVerse.commentary:
'And we have the prophetic word more fully confirmed.' The comparison here is easily misread. Peter is not saying Scripture is better evidence than his own eyes; he has just staked his case on being an eyewitness. He is saying the transfiguration confirmed the prophetic word — the voice on the mountain and the writings agree, and the readers have the writings.

Which is a considerable dignity to give a book. His readers were not on the mountain and never would be. Peter tells them that what they hold in their hands is confirmed testimony to the same thing.

'To which you will do well to pay attention as to a lamp shining in a dark place.' The image is exactly weighted. A lamp is not the sun; it is enough to see the next few feet by, and it is indispensable if the alternative is total darkness. Peter is honest about how much light Scripture gives — sufficient, and not yet daylight.

'Until the day dawns and the morning star rises in your hearts.' The lamp is temporary. There is a morning coming, and when it arrives nobody will need a lamp.

The morning star is Venus, the last light before sunrise and the herald of it — and Revelation 22:16 has Christ calling himself the bright morning star. So the dawn is his coming, which is precisely what the false teachers were denying.

'In your hearts' is the phrase that surprises. Peter has been arguing about history and testimony, and lands on the inward. The same Christ who will appear publicly is the one who rises within — and a man who has that light does not need the argument to be won before he can live by it.

verseByVerse.quote: knowing this first of all, that no prophecy of Scripture comes from someone's own interpretation. For no prophecy was ever produced by the will of man, but men spoke from God as they were carried along by the Holy Spirit.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Knowing this first of all, that no prophecy of Scripture comes from someone's own interpretation.' The verse is quoted in two directions and the context settles it.

It is often taken to mean that no individual may interpret Scripture privately. That may be a reasonable caution, but it is not what Peter is arguing here. The subject throughout is the origin of prophecy, not its later handling — and verse 21 explains verse 20 directly, beginning with 'for'.

The sense is that prophecy did not arise from the prophet's own reading of things. It was not a gifted man's insight into his times, however inspired we might loosely call that. It came from outside him.

'For no prophecy was ever produced by the will of man.' The negative is absolute — ever, and the will of man covers both intention and capacity.

'But men spoke from God as they were carried along by the Holy Spirit.' Two things held together, and the New Testament's doctrine of Scripture lives in the combination. Men spoke — real people, with their own vocabulary, style and circumstances; Isaiah does not sound like Amos. And they were carried along.

That verb is a sailing word. It is used in Acts 27 of Paul's ship, which had lost the power to steer and was driven before the wind — the sailors let her be carried along. The men are not passive cargo; they are working the vessel. But the direction is not theirs, and they arrive where the wind takes them.

Which is why the Bible reads as both thoroughly human and entirely God's word, and why Peter can appeal to it against men who were rewriting the future to suit themselves.

1.theology:
The chapter's great theological claim is 'partakers of the divine nature' (v. 4). This is not deification in the Orthodox sense (we do not become God or merge into the divine essence) nor pantheism (we do not become part of God). It is moral participation: through the Spirit and through union with Christ, God's own character — his holiness, patience, love, truthfulness — is communicated to the believer. Calvin: we are so united to Christ that we share in what belongs to him. The Reformed doctrine of sanctification is nothing less than the outworking of this participation: the divine nature expressing itself in human virtue.

The doctrine of Scripture (vv. 20–21) is equally central. Scripture is not a human document about God; it is God's own word spoken through human instruments. The Spirit carried the prophets; therefore the prophets' words carry divine authority. This is why Peter can describe the prophetic word as 'more sure' than even his own eyewitness — the written word outlasts the eyewitness, is available to all, and carries the authority not of human testimony but of the Spirit who inspired it.
1.examples:
The virtue chain (vv. 5–7) addresses a perennial pastoral problem: Christians who park at faith and see no need to move. 'I believe — isn't that enough?' Peter's answer: faith is the beginning, not the destination. A Christian who has been given the divine nature and is not building virtue, knowledge, and love is like a person given a magnificent musical instrument who never practices. The gift is real; the neglect is also real; and the result is the same — no music. The preacher should note that Peter does not make the virtues the condition of salvation (they flow from faith, not to it) but the evidence of its reality and the trajectory of its growth.

The lamp-and-morning-star image (v. 19) is a pastoral gift for believers who feel that Scripture reading is dry and unproductive. You do not read the Bible because it is always exciting; you read it because you are in a dark place and it is the only lamp available. The darkness is not a reason to put the lamp down. The lamp is precisely what a dark place requires.

2.title: The Anatomy of a False Teacher
2.text: <sup>1</sup>But false prophets also arose among the people, just as there will be false teachers among you, who will secretly bring in destructive heresies, even denying the Master who bought them, bringing upon themselves swift destruction.<sup>2</sup>And many will follow their sensuality, and because of them the way of truth will be blasphemed.<sup>3</sup>And in their greed they will exploit you with false words. Their condemnation from long ago is not idle, and their destruction is not asleep.<sup>4</sup>For if God did not spare angels when they sinned, but cast them into hell and committed them to chains of gloomy darkness to be kept until the judgment;<sup>5</sup>if he did not spare the ancient world, but preserved Noah, a herald of righteousness, with seven others, when he brought a flood upon the world of the ungodly;<sup>6</sup>if by turning the cities of Sodom and Gomorrah to ashes he condemned them to extinction, making them an example of what is going to happen to the ungodly;<sup>7</sup>and if he rescued righteous Lot, greatly distressed by the sensual conduct of the wicked<sup>8</sup>(for as that righteous man lived among them day after day, he was tormenting his righteous soul over their lawless deeds that he saw and heard);<sup>9</sup>then the Lord knows how to rescue the godly from trials, and to keep the unrighteous under punishment until the day of judgment,<sup>10</sup>and especially those who indulge in the lust of defiling passion and despise authority. Bold and willful, they do not tremble as they blaspheme the glorious ones,<sup>11</sup>whereas angels, though greater in might and power, do not pronounce a blasphemous judgment against them before the Lord.<sup>12</sup>But these, like irrational animals, creatures of instinct, born to be caught and destroyed, blaspheming about matters of which they are ignorant, will also be destroyed in their destruction,<sup>13</sup>suffering wrong as the wage for their wrongdoing. 2.overview:
Chapter 2 is Peter's sustained portrait of the false teacher — his methods (secret infiltration), his doctrine (denying the Master), his motivation (greed), and his destiny (condemnation already certain). Peter establishes the certainty of judgment through three historical examples — fallen angels, Noah's generation, Sodom and Gomorrah — and then turns to a detailed characterization of the teachers themselves: arrogant, irrational, greedy, enslaved to the very passions they indulge.

The chapter's controlling irony is in vv. 19: they promise freedom while being themselves slaves of corruption. The false teacher is always selling something he does not possess. The authentic test of any teacher is not the sophistication of his language but the shape of his life — and the false teacher's life betrays him at every point.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–10 — The Arrival and Judgment of False Teachers
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
False prophets arose among Israel, and false teachers will arise among you, smuggling in destructive heresies and denying the Master who bought them (v.1). Many will follow their sensuality, and the way of truth will be blasphemed because of them (v.2); in greed they will merchandise you with false words, and their condemnation is neither idle nor asleep (v.3).

Then a single long conditional. If God did not spare the angels who sinned but committed them to chains of gloomy darkness until judgement (v.4); if he did not spare the ancient world but preserved Noah with seven others (v.5); if he turned Sodom and Gomorrah to ashes as an example (v.6); and if he rescued righteous Lot, distressed by the conduct around him (v.7), whose righteous soul was tormented day after day by what he saw and heard (v.8) — then the Lord knows how to rescue the godly and to keep the unrighteous under punishment until the day of judgement (v.9), especially those who indulge defiling passion and despise authority (v.10).
verseByVerse.theology:
Righteous Lot

The surprise of the paragraph is that Peter calls Lot righteous three times in two verses. Genesis does not present him flatteringly: he chose the well-watered plain and pitched his tent toward Sodom, had to be dragged out by the hand while he lingered, and the story of his family afterwards is squalid.

That verdict is not sentimentality; it is the New Testament's settled way of describing people who belong to God — not on the basis of their record but of their standing. If Lot is righteous, the word cannot mean impressive. And the evidence Peter offers is entirely inward: Lot did very little, and what he did was suffer. The verb is strong — torture — and 'day after day' names the form, not one crisis but daily attrition.

Which is a genuine encouragement to a compromised believer, and Peter surely intends it. If the mark of a righteous man in Sodom is that the place still distresses him, then a reader worn down by the world around him has evidence rather than condemnation. The people who are comfortable are the ones in danger.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Note that the false teachers arise among them, twice — not attacking from outside but from within, which is what makes them dangerous and hard to name. 'Secretly bring in' means to smuggle alongside: nothing is announced, it is introduced quietly next to what is already there. And the real damage in verse 2 is not primarily to those deceived — the gospel's reputation suffers, and outsiders judge the way of truth by the people carrying its name.

Now: The three historical cases build deliberately — the highest creatures, the whole world, and the most notorious cities. If rank protected anybody it would have protected the angels, and it did not. But the second case adds the note that governs everything: God did not merely judge, he preserved, and Peter counts the survivors at eight as he did in 1 Peter 3:20. He keeps returning to how few they were. And the apodosis in verse 9 holds both halves as one skill: rescuing the godly and keeping the unrighteous are not two providences but one.

verseByVerse.quote: But false prophets also arose among the people, just as there will be false teachers among you, who will secretly bring in destructive heresies, even denying the Master who bought them, bringing upon themselves swift destruction. And many will follow their sensuality, and because of them the way of truth will be blasphemed. And in their greed they will exploit you with false words. Their condemnation from long ago is not idle, and their destruction is not asleep.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'But false prophets also arose among the people, just as there will be false teachers among you.' The parallel is the argument. Israel had them; the church will have them. Peter offers the pattern as a warning rather than a novelty — nobody should be surprised.

And note among, twice. Not attacking from outside but arising from within, which is what makes them dangerous and hard to name.

'Who will secretly bring in destructive heresies.' The verb means to smuggle alongside. Nothing is announced; it is introduced quietly next to what is already there, and the word for heresies means chosen opinions — a man's own preference set up against what was delivered.

'Even denying the Master who bought them.' Master is despotes, the owner of slaves — and 'bought' is the slave-market word again. The picture is of purchased slaves repudiating the man who paid for them.

The phrase raises a real question about whether Christ died for those finally lost, and honesty is better than a quick answer. Peter is not writing a treatise on the extent of the atonement; he is using the language of ownership to make the ingratitude vivid. These men stood within the covenant community and enjoyed everything that came with it, and turned on the one who purchased it — which is the offence he wants felt.

'And many will follow their sensuality, and because of them the way of truth will be blasphemed.' That is the real damage, and it is not primarily to those who are deceived. The gospel's reputation suffers. Outsiders judge the way of truth by the people carrying its name, and this letter's readers were already being slandered.

'In their greed they will exploit you with false words.' The motive is money, as it was in 1 Timothy 6:5 — and 'exploit' is a trading word: they will merchandise you. The congregation is the commodity.

'Their condemnation from long ago is not idle, and their destruction is not asleep.' Both images personify judgement as something awake and moving. It has been on its way for a long time and has not stopped.

verseByVerse.quote: For if God did not spare angels when they sinned, but cast them into hell and committed them to chains of gloomy darkness to be kept until the judgment; if he did not spare the ancient world, but preserved Noah, a herald of righteousness, with seven others, when he brought a flood upon the world of the ungodly; if by turning the cities of Sodom and Gomorrah to ashes he condemned them to extinction, making them an example of what is going to happen to the ungodly;
verseByVerse.commentary:
Peter now argues from history, and the sentence is a single long conditional running from verse 4 to verse 9: if… if… if… then. Three cases, and each supplies something.

'If God did not spare angels when they sinned.' The first case is the highest of creatures. If rank protected anybody it would have protected them, and it did not. The word translated hell here is tartaros, used only here in the New Testament — a term from Greek mythology for the deepest place of confinement, which Peter borrows the way he borrowed the mystery-cult word in 1:16.

'Committed them to chains of gloomy darkness to be kept until the judgment.' Note that it is custody rather than sentence. They are held for a trial that has not yet happened.

'If he did not spare the ancient world, but preserved Noah, a herald of righteousness, with seven others.' The second case adds the note that will govern the whole argument: God did not merely judge — he preserved. And Peter counts the survivors: eight, as in 1 Peter 3:20. He keeps returning to how few they were.

'Herald of righteousness' is an interesting description, since Genesis records no sermon of Noah's. Peter, or the tradition he knows, understands the building of the ark itself as a proclamation — a hundred years of hammering in the sight of neighbours who thought him mad.

'If by turning the cities of Sodom and Gomorrah to ashes he condemned them to extinction, making them an example.' The third case is the most public. The word for example means a pattern set out for others to look at, and the ruins by the Dead Sea functioned that way in Jewish memory for centuries.

So the three build: the highest creatures, the whole world, and the most notorious cities. If none of those was spared, the case Peter is making does not need arguing further.

verseByVerse.quote: and if he rescued righteous Lot, greatly distressed by the sensual conduct of the wicked (for as that righteous man lived among them day after day, he was tormenting his righteous soul over their lawless deeds that he saw and heard); then the Lord knows how to rescue the godly from trials, and to keep the unrighteous under punishment until the day of judgment,
verseByVerse.commentary:
'And if he rescued righteous Lot.' This is the surprise of the paragraph, and it is worth pausing on, because Genesis does not present Lot flatteringly. He chose the well-watered plain and pitched his tent toward Sodom; he had to be dragged out by the hand while he lingered; and the story of his family afterwards is squalid.

Peter calls him righteous three times in two verses.

That is a remarkable verdict, and it is not sentimentality. It is the New Testament's settled way of describing people who belong to God — not on the basis of their record but of their standing. If Lot is righteous, the word cannot mean impressive.

'Greatly distressed by the sensual conduct of the wicked.' Here is the evidence Peter goes on, and it is entirely inward. Lot did very little; what he did was suffer. And verse 8 says it twice more: 'as that righteous man lived among them day after day, he was tormenting his righteous soul over their lawless deeds that he saw and heard.'

The verb is strong — torture. And 'day after day' names the form it took: not one crisis but daily attrition, a man who had chosen to live there and could not stop being grieved by it.

Which is a genuine encouragement to a compromised believer, and Peter surely intends it. If the mark of a righteous man in Sodom is that the place still distresses him, then the reader who feels worn down by the world around him has evidence rather than condemnation. The people who are comfortable are the ones in danger.

'Then the Lord knows how to rescue the godly from trials, and to keep the unrighteous under punishment.' The apodosis at last, and both halves matter. He knows how — the competence is his, and the readers do not have to work out the mechanism. And the same providence does both: rescuing and keeping are one skill, not two.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 11–22 — The Portrait, and the Washed Sow
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Angels, though greater in might, do not pronounce blasphemous judgement (v.11); but these, like irrational creatures of instinct, blaspheme what they do not understand and will be destroyed (v.12), revelling in the daytime, blots and blemishes feasting with you (v.13), with eyes full of adultery, enticing unsteady souls, hearts trained in greed (v.14). They have followed the way of Balaam, who loved gain from wrongdoing (v.15), and was rebuked by a speechless donkey that restrained the prophet's madness (v.16).

They are waterless springs and storm-driven mists, for whom utter darkness is reserved (v.17), enticing by sensual passions those barely escaping from error (v.18), promising freedom while being slaves of corruption — for whatever overcomes a person enslaves him (v.19). If after escaping the world's defilements through knowledge of Christ they are again entangled and overcome, the last state is worse than the first (v.20); better never to have known the way of righteousness than to turn back (v.21). The proverb has come true of them: the dog returns to its vomit, and the washed sow to the mire (v.22).
verseByVerse.theology:
Washed, Not Changed

Verses 20-21 are among the most sobering in the New Testament and must be allowed their weight. The language of escape and knowledge is real: whatever these men were, they were not outsiders. And the Lord said the same about a house swept clean and reoccupied, so that the last state is worse than the first (Matt 12:45).

How this stands with perseverance is answered by Peter himself in verse 22, which is why the proverb is there. Look at what has and has not changed. The sow has been washed — genuinely, outwardly, and everyone could see it. What she has not been given is a different nature. She returns to the mud because she is still a pig, and washing a pig does not make it a sheep. That is Peter's verdict: not that they lost salvation, but that they were cleaned rather than changed — exactly what 1 John 2:19 says of those who went out from us because they were not of us.

The pastoral use is not to make secure believers anxious but to make everyone honest. The question is not whether you have been washed, but whether you have been changed — and the evidence is what you find yourself returning to.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Balaam is the exact case: a genuine prophet who put his gift on the market. He was not deceived — he had heard from God repeatedly and went anyway, which is why Peter calls it madness rather than error. The Greek of verse 16 is pointed: a voiceless beast producing a human voice, because the prophet is behaving like an animal and an animal has to do the prophet's job. There is mercy in the story too, easily missed — the donkey and the angel were sent to stop him.

Now: Verse 19 contains one of the truest sentences in the letter: 'whatever overcomes a person, to that he is enslaved.' Freedom is not the absence of a master but a question of which one, and the man who throws off restraint has not become free — he has changed owners and taken a worse one. Note too who is targeted in verse 18: people 'barely escaping', new converts still unsteady, who have just broken with a way of life at real cost and are told they need not have bothered. And it is done with 'loud boasts' — delivered confidently, which is what makes it work on the unsure.

verseByVerse.quote: and especially those who indulge in the lust of defiling passion and despise authority. Bold and willful, they do not tremble as they blaspheme the glorious ones, whereas angels, though greater in might and power, do not pronounce a blasphemous judgment against them before the Lord.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'And especially those who indulge in the lust of defiling passion and despise authority.' Two marks, and the second is the one Peter develops. These men will not be told anything by anybody.

'Bold and willful.' The first word means daring, the second self-pleasing — literally self-satisfied. Together they describe a confidence that has no external check on it, which is exactly what makes a false teacher persuasive.

'They do not tremble as they blaspheme the glorious ones.' The glorious ones are almost certainly angelic beings, and the point is not what they said but the ease with which they said it. They speak about the unseen world casually, as men who have never considered that it might be real.

Then the comparison, and it is devastating: 'whereas angels, though greater in might and power, do not pronounce a blasphemous judgment against them before the Lord.'

Angels — who actually know what these powers are, and who outrank the men entirely — will not speak that way. Jude's parallel makes it sharper still: Michael the archangel, disputing about the body of Moses, would not pronounce a reviling judgement but said 'the Lord rebuke you' (Jude 9).

So the contrast is between beings who have seen the reality and are careful, and men who have seen nothing and are careless. Ignorance is producing the confidence.

And there is a lesson in it that outlives the original situation. A settled reverence about what one does not understand is a mark of spiritual maturity, and a readiness to talk loosely about the unseen is usually a sign of having thought about it very little.

verseByVerse.quote: But these, like irrational animals, creatures of instinct, born to be caught and destroyed, blaspheming about matters of which they are ignorant, will also be destroyed in their destruction, suffering wrong as the wage for their wrongdoing. They count it pleasure to revel in the daytime. They are blots and blemishes, reveling in their deceptions, while they feast with you. They have eyes full of adultery, insatiable for sin. They entice unsteady souls. They have hearts trained in greed. Accursed children!
verseByVerse.commentary:
'But these, like irrational animals, creatures of instinct.' The comparison is not merely abusive; it is diagnostic. An animal acts on appetite without deliberation, and Peter says that is precisely how these men operate. They have exchanged reason for instinct, which is why arguing with them achieves nothing.

'Blaspheming about matters of which they are ignorant.' The charge of verse 10 restated, with the cause named: ignorance. And 'will also be destroyed in their destruction' — the ruin they bring is the ruin they receive.

'They count it pleasure to revel in the daytime.' A precise cultural detail. Even by the standards of a Greek city, serious drinking belonged to the night; daytime revelling was the mark of a man who had abandoned all restraint. Paul says the same — those who get drunk are drunk at night (1 Thess 5:7).

'They are blots and blemishes, reveling in their deceptions, while they feast with you.' There is the sting. This is happening at the church's own meal — most likely the love feast that accompanied the Lord's Supper. And blots and blemishes is a deliberate reversal: 1 Peter 1:19 described Christ as a lamb without blemish or spot, and these men are the opposite, sitting at his table.

'They have eyes full of adultery, insatiable for sin.' The Greek is vivid — eyes full of an adulteress, a man who cannot look at a woman without assessing her.

'They entice unsteady souls.' The verb is the fishing word: baited. And the target is named — unsteady, unstable, the people not yet firm. Predators select carefully.

'They have hearts trained in greed.' Trained is the athlete's word, the root of gymnasium. Greed has been practised until it is skilled — this is not a lapse but a discipline, worked at until it comes naturally.

verseByVerse.quote: Forsaking the right way, they have gone astray. They have followed the way of Balaam, the son of Beor, who loved gain from wrongdoing, but was rebuked for his own transgression; a speechless donkey spoke with human voice and restrained the prophet's madness.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Forsaking the right way, they have gone astray. They have followed the way of Balaam.' Peter names the pattern, and Balaam is the exact case: a genuine prophet who put his gift on the market.

The story is in Numbers 22-24. Balak of Moab offers money to have Israel cursed; Balaam keeps asking God for permission to go, and the narrative makes plain that he wants the fee. In the end he cannot curse — but he later advises Moab how to seduce Israel into sin instead (Num 31:16), which is what he is remembered for.

'Who loved gain from wrongdoing.' That is Peter's summary, and it identifies the false teachers precisely: not men who set out to destroy the church but men who discovered that religion pays and adjusted their message to keep it paying.

Then verse 16, and Peter tells it with a certain relish: 'but was rebuked for his own transgression; a speechless donkey spoke with human voice and restrained the prophet's madness.'

The Greek is pointed — a voiceless beast of burden producing a human voice, and the reversal is the joke. The prophet is behaving like an animal, so an animal has to do the prophet's job.

'The prophet's madness.' A hard word, and Peter chooses it deliberately. Balaam was not deceived; he had heard from God repeatedly and went anyway. That is not error, it is derangement — and the man who knows exactly what God has said and calculates that the money is worth it has lost his reason, whatever his gifts.

There is a mercy in the story too, easily missed. The donkey and the angel were sent to stop him. Even a man this far gone was given an obstacle in the road.

verseByVerse.quote: These are waterless springs and mists driven by a storm. For them the gloom of utter darkness has been reserved. For, speaking loud boasts of folly, they entice by sensual passions of the flesh those who are barely escaping from those who live in error. They promise them freedom, but they themselves are slaves of corruption. For whatever overcomes a person, to that he is enslaved.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'These are waterless springs and mists driven by a storm.' Two images, and both are about promise without delivery.

In that country a spring was life. To walk to one in the heat and find it dry is not disappointment but danger — and Peter is describing men whose teaching offers exactly what a thirsty person needs and has nothing in it.

The second is the same failure in the sky. Clouds driven by a squall raise every farmer's hope and pass over without rain, and Jude uses the same picture (Jude 12). These men are weather that does not break.

'For them the gloom of utter darkness has been reserved.' The word 'reserved' is the custody word from verse 4 — kept, set aside. And there is a grim fitness: men who promised light are held in the dark.

'Speaking loud boasts of folly, they entice by sensual passions of the flesh those who are barely escaping from those who live in error.' The method is stated exactly. The bait is not intellectual — it is appetite — and the target is people who have only just got out.

That is the cruelty of it. New converts, still unsteady, having just broken with a way of life at real cost, are told they need not have bothered. And it is done with 'loud boasts' — the promise is delivered confidently, which is what makes it work on people who are unsure.

'They promise them freedom, but they themselves are slaves of corruption.' The irony is the sharpest thing in the chapter. And the principle Peter draws is one of the truest sentences in the letter: 'whatever overcomes a person, to that he is enslaved.' Freedom is not the absence of a master; it is a question of which one. The man who has thrown off restraint has not become free — he has changed owners, and taken a worse one.

verseByVerse.quote: For if, after they have escaped the defilements of the world through the knowledge of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ, they are again entangled in them and overcome, the last state has become worse for them than the first. For it would have been better for them never to have known the way of righteousness than after knowing it to turn back from the holy commandment delivered to them. What the true proverb says has happened to them: "The dog returns to its own vomit, and the sow, after washing herself, returns to wallow in the mire."
verseByVerse.commentary:
These verses are among the most sobering in the New Testament, and they must be allowed their weight before anything is done to soften them.

'If, after they have escaped the defilements of the world through the knowledge of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ, they are again entangled in them and overcome, the last state has become worse for them than the first.' The language of escape and knowledge is real. Whatever these men were, they were not outsiders — they had genuinely got out, and genuinely knew.

The Lord said the same about a house swept clean and reoccupied by seven worse spirits, so that the last state is worse than the first (Matt 12:45). Peter is quoting his Master.

'It would have been better for them never to have known the way of righteousness than after knowing it to turn back.' That is the plain sense and it should not be blunted. Knowledge raises the stakes; a man who has seen and turned away is in a worse position than one who never saw.

How does this stand with the perseverance of the saints? Peter himself supplies the answer in verse 22, and it is the reason the proverb is there.

'The dog returns to its own vomit, and the sow, after washing herself, returns to wallow in the mire.' Look at what has and has not changed. The sow has been washed — genuinely, outwardly, and everyone could see it. What she has not been given is a different nature. She returns to the mud because she is still a pig, and washing a pig does not make it a sheep.

That is Peter's verdict on such men: not that they lost salvation, but that they were cleaned rather than changed. The escape was real at the level of behaviour and the heart was never renewed — which is exactly what 1 John 2:19 says of those who went out from us because they were not of us.

And the pastoral use is not to make secure believers anxious but to make everyone honest. The question the chapter puts is not whether you have been washed. It is whether you have been changed, and the evidence is what you find yourself returning to.

2.theology: The chapter's controlling theological question is the nature of apostasy. Can a person who has genuinely known Christ fall finally away? The Reformed answer: those truly regenerate will persevere (John 10:28–29; Rom 8:38–39). But the visible church contains those who participate in covenant privileges without possessing covenant life — and it is these who can experience the knowledge described in v. 20 and still return to their former state. The dog and pig proverbs define the boundary: the animal's nature is unchanged. External reformation without regeneration leads to greater corruption. This is not a loophole in the doctrine of perseverance; it is the doctrine's honest context.
2.examples: The Balaam portrait (vv. 15–16) gives the congregation diagnostic tools. The false teacher's test is not doctrinal sophistication but financial transparency: What does this teacher gain from what he teaches? Is the teaching shaped by what people want to hear (and therefore what they will pay to hear)? Balaam was a genuine prophet whose gift was real — but the gift became a commodity. The test of authentic ministry is not whether the gifts are real but whether the teacher loves the Lord more than the wages.

3.title: The Day That Is Coming
3.overview:
The final chapter is the letter's destination. Everything in chapters 1 and 2 has been preparation for this: the false teachers are dangerous not merely because they are immoral but because they have attacked the hope — the promise of Christ's return — and by doing so have severed the ethical nerve of the Christian life. If the Day is not coming, why be holy? If the Lord will not appear, why resist the flesh? The scoffers have grasped this logic and pressed it into service of their own licentiousness.

Peter's response is one of the most carefully constructed arguments in the New Testament. He does not simply reassert the promise; he dismantles the philosophical framework on which the denial rests. The scoffers appeal to uniformitarianism: 'all things are continuing as they were from the beginning of creation' (v. 4). The world operates by uniform natural processes; there is no basis for expecting a divine interruption. Peter's counter-attack is historical and theological: the world has already been interrupted — twice — by the word of God (creation from water, and the flood), and the same word that brought those interventions has promised a third. Uniformitarianism has already been falsified by the history the scoffers claim to cite.

Then comes the pastoral heart of the chapter — the motive for the apparent delay. God is not slow. He is patient — long-suffering, holding back His power — because He is 'not willing that any should perish, but that all should reach repentance' (v. 9). The delay is not absence. It is mercy. Every day before the Day is a day of grace, an open door of repentance. When the Day comes — sudden, certain, like a thief — it will be final. But it will come into a world still being offered the gospel, and that is the point.

The chapter closes with what may be the most ethically charged question in the epistle: 'What sort of people ought you to be?' (v. 11). Not: When will it happen? The return of Christ is not a date to calculate but a character to cultivate. Holiness, godliness, eagerness for the Day, diligence to be found spotless — this is the life shaped by a hope that is certain. And the letter ends where it began: grow in the grace and knowledge of our Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ. To him be the glory both now and to the day of eternity.

In both of them I am stirring up your sincere mind by way of reminder,<sup>2</sup>that you should remember the predictions of the holy prophets and the commandment of the Lord and Savior through your apostles,<sup>3</sup>knowing this first of all, that scoffers will come in the last days with scoffing, following their own sinful desires.<sup>4</sup>They will say, "Where is the promise of his coming?
