verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–10 — The Scoffers and the Day
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
This second letter, like the first, stirs up their sincere mind by reminder (v.1), that they may remember the prophets and the Lord's commandment through their apostles (v.2), knowing that scoffers will come in the last days following their own desires (v.3), saying, 'Where is the promise of his coming? Everything continues as it has from the beginning' (v.4).

They deliberately overlook that the heavens existed long ago and the earth was formed out of water by God's word (v.5), and that by these the world then existing was deluged and perished (v.6); and that by the same word the present heavens and earth are stored up for fire, kept until the day of judgement (v.7). But do not overlook this: with the Lord one day is as a thousand years and a thousand years as one day (v.8). The Lord is not slow but patient, not wishing any to perish but all to reach repentance (v.9). Yet the day will come like a thief; the heavens will pass away with a roar, the elements dissolve, and the earth and its works be laid bare (v.10).
verseByVerse.theology:
Not Slowness but Patience

Verse 8 is not a formula for calculating prophetic timescales, and reading it as one has produced a great deal of nonsense. The comparison runs both ways, which makes any arithmetic useless. What it says is that God does not stand inside time as we do: to a creature with sixty years a delay of two millennia is decisive; to the one who made time it is not a delay at all. And both halves are needed — a thousand years as one day means the long wait is nothing to him, while one day as a thousand years means no single day is trivial to him either. He is not inattentive during the interval.

Verse 9 has been fought over for centuries and honesty serves better than a slogan. Some read 'any' and 'all' as universal, and Scripture elsewhere speaks that way (Ezek 33:11; 1 Tim 2:4). Others note that Peter writes to a specific church and says 'patient toward you', so that 'all' most naturally means all his own, the delay existing so that none of the elect is missing. The second fits the immediate grammar better, the first the wider scriptural language about God's disposition. What neither permits is the scoffers' conclusion — that the delay means nothing is coming. And on either reading the pastoral use is identical: if God is holding the door open, the response of anyone still outside is not to argue about the mechanism but to walk through.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The scoffers' argument has two parts and both would have stung. The first generation had died and nothing had happened — a real problem in a church burying its founders. The second is a philosophy: the world is a closed system of unbroken regularity, so what has never been observed does not happen. That is a strikingly modern argument to find in a first-century letter. Peter does not dispute the observation; he disputes the conclusion, naming two occasions when things did not continue as they were — and both are in the Scriptures the scoffers claimed to respect.

Now: The last clause of verse 10 is the most important in it. The best manuscripts read found or laid bare rather than 'burned up', which changes the picture from destruction to disclosure: the fire is not chiefly an incinerator but a searchlight. That is far more searching than annihilation would be — a universe that simply burns cancels the record, while a universe laid bare produces it. Against men living as they pleased on the assumption that nothing was coming, Peter's point is not that the world will end but that it will be examined.

verseByVerse.quote: This is now the second letter that I am writing to you, beloved. In both of them I am stirring up your sincere mind by way of reminder, that you should remember the predictions of the holy prophets and the commandment of the Lord and Savior through your apostles,
verseByVerse.commentary:
'This is now the second letter that I am writing to you.' Peter identifies himself as the author of 1 Peter and treats both letters as one project with one aim.

'In both of them I am stirring up your sincere mind by way of reminder.' The waking verb again from 1:13. Peter's settled view of his ministry is that his readers do not need new material; they need rousing.

'Sincere' is a striking word here. It translates a term that may derive from testing pottery by holding it up to sunlight to see whether cracks had been filled with wax — what a thing appears to be when the light gets behind it. Peter credits them with genuineness even as he warns them.

'That you should remember the predictions of the holy prophets and the commandment of the Lord and Savior through your apostles.' Two authorities, set side by side without any suggestion that they differ in weight: the Old Testament prophets, and the apostles carrying the Lord's own commandment.

That is a significant sentence for how the early church understood its own writings. Peter puts apostolic teaching in the same bracket as prophetic Scripture — and he will do it explicitly with Paul's letters in verse 16.

Note also 'your apostles'. Not a distant institution but the men who actually brought them the gospel. And the whole defence against what follows is memory — not a new argument but the recollection of what they were already told.

verseByVerse.quote: knowing this first of all, that scoffers will come in the last days with scoffing, following their own sinful desires. They will say, "Where is the promise of his coming? For ever since the fathers fell asleep, all things are continuing as they were from the beginning of creation."
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Knowing this first of all, that scoffers will come in the last days with scoffing.' The construction is emphatic — mockers mocking — and Peter says their arrival is itself predicted. That is a quietly clever move: the appearance of people denying the promise is evidence that the promise was accurately given.

'Following their own sinful desires.' Peter names the motive before he states the argument, and the order is deliberate. Their doctrine has a cause, and the cause is not intellectual. A man who wants the future to be empty has a reason for wanting it.

Then the taunt itself: 'Where is the promise of his coming?'

'For ever since the fathers fell asleep, all things are continuing as they were from the beginning of creation.' The argument has two parts and both would have stung. The first generation has died and nothing has happened — a real pastoral problem in a church burying its founders.

And the second is a philosophy: things go on as they always have. It is the assumption that the world is a closed system running on unbroken regularity, and that what has never been observed to happen therefore does not happen. That is a very modern-sounding argument to find in a first-century letter.

Peter's answer, when it comes, does not dispute the observation. He disputes the conclusion — and he does it by pointing to two occasions when things did not continue as they were.

verseByVerse.quote: For they deliberately overlook this fact, that the heavens existed long ago, and the earth was formed out of water and through water by the word of God, and that by means of these the world that then existed was deluged with water and perished. But by the same word the heavens and earth that now exist are stored up for fire, being kept until the day of judgment and destruction of the ungodly.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'For they deliberately overlook this fact.' The verb means this escapes them by their own choosing — it is willed forgetfulness. Peter does not accuse them of missing the evidence but of declining to look at it, which is the more serious charge.

And what they overlook is creation itself: 'the heavens existed long ago, and the earth was formed out of water and through water by the word of God.' The claim that all things continue as they were from the beginning of creation collapses at the word creation. There was a beginning, and it was not a continuation of anything.

'And that by means of these the world that then existed was deluged with water and perished.' The second interruption. The same water that the world was formed through later destroyed it — which is exactly a case of things not continuing as they were.

So the argument is complete in two strokes. The scoffers say nothing has ever interrupted the regularity; Peter names two occasions when the world's entire state was changed by the word of God, and both are in the Scriptures the scoffers claim to respect.

'But by the same word the heavens and earth that now exist are stored up for fire.' The phrase 'the same word' is the hinge of the whole passage. One agency made it, one flooded it, and one holds it now. The present stability is not inertia; it is sustained, and by the same voice that could end it.

'Being kept until the day of judgment.' The custody word again, as of the angels in 2:4. Peter's picture of the present universe is not a machine running down but something held in reserve.

verseByVerse.quote: But do not overlook this one fact, beloved, that with the Lord one day is as a thousand years, and a thousand years as one day.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'But do not overlook this one fact, beloved.' The same verb he used of the scoffers, now turned round with an endearment attached. They deliberately overlook; do not you overlook this.

'That with the Lord one day is as a thousand years, and a thousand years as one day.' The line echoes Psalm 90:4, and it is the answer to the delay — though not the answer usually taken from it.

It is not a formula for calculating prophetic timescales. Peter is not supplying a conversion rate, and reading it as one has produced a great deal of nonsense. Notice that the comparison runs both ways, which would make any arithmetic useless: a day is as a thousand years and a thousand years as a day.

What it says is that God does not stand inside time as we do. To a creature with sixty or eighty years, a delay of two millennia is decisive; to the one who made time it is not a delay at all. The scoffers' argument depends entirely on assuming God experiences duration the way they do.

And both halves are needed. A thousand years as one day means the long wait is nothing to him. One day as a thousand years means no single day is trivial to him either — he is not distracted or inattentive during the interval.

Which removes the sting from the taunt without pretending the wait is short. The fathers did fall asleep, and centuries have passed since Peter wrote. The question is only whether that fact means what the scoffers said it meant, and this verse says it does not.

verseByVerse.quote: The Lord is not slow to fulfill his promise as some count slowness, but is patient toward you, not wishing that any should perish, but that all should reach repentance.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'The Lord is not slow to fulfil his promise as some count slowness.' Peter denies the premise directly, and note the qualifier: as some count. The slowness exists only in the reckoning of the people complaining.

'But is patient toward you.' And here is the positive answer, which is the great sentence of the chapter. The delay is not indifference, not incapacity, and not forgetfulness. It is patience — and it is directed at them.

That reframes the whole complaint. Every day the end has not come is a day granted. The scoffers were treating the interval as evidence against God; Peter says it is evidence of his mercy, and that they are standing inside the very thing they are mocking.

'Not wishing that any should perish, but that all should reach repentance.' The verse has been fought over for centuries and honesty serves better than a slogan.

Some read 'any' and 'all' as universal — God desires the salvation of every person without exception, and Scripture elsewhere speaks that way (Ezek 33:11; 1 Tim 2:4). Others note that Peter is writing to a specific church and says 'patient toward you', so that the 'all' most naturally means all of you, all his own — and that the delay exists so that none of the elect is missing when the day comes.

The second reading fits the immediate grammar better; the first fits the wider scriptural language about God's disposition toward sinners. What neither reading permits is the conclusion the scoffers wanted — that the delay means nothing is coming.

And on either reading the pastoral use is identical, which is presumably why Peter wrote it. If God is holding the door open, the response of anyone still outside it is not to argue about the mechanism but to walk through.

verseByVerse.quote: But the day of the Lord will come like a thief, and then the heavens will pass away with a roar, and the heavenly bodies will be burned up and dissolved, and the earth and the works that are done on it will be exposed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'But the day of the Lord will come like a thief.' The image is the Lord's own (Matt 24:43), and Paul uses it too. What it conveys is not stealth for its own sake but unpredictability — the one thing about a burglary that you cannot prepare for is the timing.

Which answers the scoffers' question exactly. They asked where the promise was; Peter says the promise includes the fact that you will not see it coming.

'Then the heavens will pass away with a roar.' The word is onomatopoeic — a rushing, hissing, crackling noise, used of the whirring of wings and the sound of flames. Peter's universe does not end quietly.

'The heavenly bodies will be burned up and dissolved.' The word for heavenly bodies is stoicheia, the elements — which may mean the celestial lights, or the basic constituents of the material world. Either way the dissolution is total.

Then the last clause, and it is the most important in the verse: 'and the earth and the works that are done on it will be exposed.'

The best manuscripts read found or laid bare rather than 'burned up', and it changes the picture from mere destruction to disclosure. The fire is not chiefly an incinerator but a searchlight. Everything done on this earth will be found out.

And that is a far more searching thought than annihilation would be. A universe that simply burns cancels the record; a universe that is laid bare produces it. Peter's point against men who were living as they pleased on the assumption that nothing was coming is not that the world will end but that it will be examined.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 11–18 — New Heavens, and the Last Command
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Since all these things are to be dissolved, what sort of people ought you to be in lives of holiness and godliness (v.11), waiting for and hastening the day of God, when the heavens will be set on fire and the elements melt (v.12)? But according to his promise we wait for new heavens and a new earth in which righteousness dwells (v.13).

Therefore be diligent to be found by him without spot or blemish, and at peace (v.14), counting the Lord's patience as salvation — as Paul also wrote according to the wisdom given him (v.15), in all his letters, in which some things are hard to understand and which the ignorant and unstable twist to their own destruction, as they do the other Scriptures (v.16). Knowing this beforehand, take care not to be carried away by the error of lawless people and lose your stability (v.17); but grow in the grace and knowledge of our Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ, to whom be glory now and to the day of eternity (v.18).
verseByVerse.theology:
The Answer to Error Is Growth

After two chapters of warning, the last command is not what one expects. Peter does not end by telling them to watch the heretics more closely; he tells them to get on with maturing. A tree that is growing is far harder to uproot than one being braced.

And both nouns matter. Grace — because a man who forgets he was cleansed stops growing (1:9). And knowledge — the letter's key word, reclaimed one last time from the men peddling a counterfeit. The answer to false knowledge is not less knowledge but the real thing, and it is knowledge of a person. Note also the doxology addressed to Christ, which is itself a statement about who he is, and the phrase 'the day of eternity', found nowhere else: having written a chapter about the day of the Lord and the day of judgement, Peter ends by naming a day that does not end.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Peter's warmth toward Paul in verse 15 repays pausing on. These two had a serious public disagreement at Antioch, where Paul opposed him to his face and later wrote it down (Gal 2:11-14). Peter calls him beloved brother and commends his wisdom, with no trace of the quarrel. He also admits, refreshingly, that some of Paul is hard to understand — a small comfort to anyone who has struggled through Romans — while noting that difficulty is not the cause of the twisting: the ignorant and unstable are, and they do it to the plain parts too. And in the same breath he calls Paul's letters Scripture, very likely while Paul was still alive. That is the New Testament recognising itself.

Now: 'Hastening' in verse 12 is startling. Its ordinary sense is to speed something up — and Peter has just said the delay is God's patience, waiting for people to reach repentance. If that is why he waits, the church's own repentance and mission are bound up with the timing, which gives ordinary Christian obedience a dignity that should stop anyone reading it casually. And verse 13 turns the bleakness round: the fire is not the end of the story, and what follows is a new earth — physical, real, renewed, as Isaiah promised (Isa 65:17) — 'in which righteousness dwells', at home rather than visiting. That is the answer to everything chapter 2 described.

verseByVerse.quote: Since all these things are thus to be dissolved, what sort of people ought you to be in lives of holiness and godliness, waiting for and hastening the coming of the day of God, because of which the heavens will be set on fire and dissolved, and the heavenly bodies will melt as they burn! But according to his promise we are waiting for new heavens and a new earth in which righteousness dwells.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Since all these things are thus to be dissolved, what sort of people ought you to be?' Peter draws the practical conclusion, and it is worth noticing what he does not draw. Not speculation, not date-setting, not withdrawal. What sort of people ought you to be — the question is about character.

'In lives of holiness and godliness.' Both nouns are plural in Greek — holy behaviours, godlinesses — which suggests the concrete and repeated rather than a general disposition. It is worked out in particular acts.

'Waiting for and hastening the coming of the day of God.' The second verb is startling. It can mean to be eager for, but its ordinary sense is to speed something up — and Peter has just said the delay is God's patience, waiting for people to reach repentance. If that is why he waits, then the church's own work of repentance and mission is bound up with the timing. That is a dignity given to ordinary Christian obedience which should stop anyone reading it casually.

'Because of which the heavens will be set on fire and dissolved.' The description is repeated, and it is bleak — until verse 13 turns it round.

'But according to his promise we are waiting for new heavens and a new earth.' There is the point of the whole passage. The fire is not the end of the story and it is not the destruction of the material world as such. What follows is a new earth — physical, real, and renewed, exactly as Isaiah promised (Isa 65:17).

'In which righteousness dwells.' And that single clause is the answer to everything chapter 2 described. Peter has spent a chapter on men who exploited the church and got away with it. The world that is coming is one where righteousness is not visiting but resident — at home, which is the force of the verb.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore, beloved, since you are waiting for these, be diligent to be found by him without spot or blemish, and at peace. And count the patience of our Lord as salvation, just as our beloved brother Paul also wrote to you according to the wisdom given him, as he does in all his letters when he speaks in them of these matters. There are some things in them that are hard to understand, which the ignorant and unstable twist to their own destruction, as they do the other Scriptures.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Therefore, beloved, since you are waiting for these, be diligent to be found by him without spot or blemish, and at peace.'

'Found' picks up the word from verse 10, where the earth and its works are laid bare. The same verb, and the connection is deliberate: everything will be found out, so be diligent about what is found in you.

And 'without spot or blemish' is another deliberate reversal. The false teachers were 'blots and blemishes' at the church's own feast (2:13); the readers are to be the opposite, which is the description given to Christ himself as the lamb (1 Pet 1:19).

'And count the patience of our Lord as salvation.' Verse 9 restated as a command. The delay is not to be endured but reckoned — actively counted as mercy. It is the accounting verb, and Peter asks them to enter the interval on the right side of the ledger.

'Just as our beloved brother Paul also wrote to you.' Peter's warmth here is worth pausing on. These two men had a serious public disagreement at Antioch, where Paul opposed him to his face and later wrote it down (Gal 2:11-14). Peter calls him beloved brother and commends his wisdom. There is no trace of the quarrel.

'There are some things in them that are hard to understand.' A refreshingly honest admission from an apostle about another apostle, and a small comfort to anyone who has struggled through Romans.

'Which the ignorant and unstable twist to their own destruction, as they do the other Scriptures.' Two things follow. Difficulty is not the cause of the twisting — the ignorant and unstable are, and they do it to the plain parts too. And Peter has just called Paul's letters Scripture, while Paul was very likely still alive. That is the New Testament recognising itself.

verseByVerse.quote: You therefore, beloved, knowing this beforehand, take care that you are not carried away with the error of lawless people and lose your own stability. But grow in the grace and knowledge of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ. To him be the glory both now and to the day of eternity. Amen.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'You therefore, beloved, knowing this beforehand, take care.' The whole letter's purpose in a phrase. Peter has not written to inform them about the future but to prepare them, and forewarning is itself the protection.

'That you are not carried away with the error of lawless people and lose your own stability.' The verb 'carried away' is the same one Paul used of Barnabas being led astray at Antioch. And stability is the answer to a word that has run through the letter: the unstable souls the false teachers baited (2:14), and the unstable who twist the Scriptures (3:16). Peter's fear is that the steady will be pulled into that instability.

Then the last command, and after two chapters of warning it is not what one expects: 'But grow in the grace and knowledge of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ.'

The defence against error is not chiefly vigilance but growth. Peter does not end by telling them to watch the heretics more closely; he tells them to get on with maturing. A tree that is growing is far harder to uproot than one being braced.

And both nouns matter. Grace — because a man who forgets he was cleansed stops growing (1:9). And knowledge — the letter's key word, gnosis, reclaimed one last time from the men who were peddling a counterfeit. The answer to false knowledge is not less knowledge but the real thing, and it is knowledge of a person.

'To him be the glory both now and to the day of eternity. Amen.' A doxology addressed to Christ, which is itself a statement about who he is. And the phrase 'the day of eternity' occurs nowhere else — Peter, having written a chapter about the day of the Lord and the day of judgement, ends by naming a day that does not end.

These are the last recorded words of the man who denied his Lord in a courtyard, written by someone who knew his death was near. He signs off with glory to the one he had once said he did not know.

3.theology:
Uniformitarianism and the Word of God: Peter's refutation of the scoffers in vv. 5–7 is a model of theological apologetics. The uniformitarians claim that the world operates by consistent natural processes. Peter grants the observation and then shows that the historical record — the record the uniformitarians themselves appeal to — contains two catastrophic interruptions of the very uniformity they invoke: creation and the flood. Both were brought about by the word of God. The same word that did those things has spoken again, and the third act — the fire — is as certain as the first two. The apologist who begins with Scripture's own historical witness is standing on solid ground.

Divine patience and the will of God in salvation: Verse 9 is one of the great texts on the scope of God's salvific will: 'not wishing that any should perish, but that all should reach repentance.' Reformed theology reads this in its literary context: 'toward you' — the elect community. The 'all' is the full complement of those for whom God's patience is being exercised — all who will come to repentance within the span of His patience. This is not universalism (the Day will still come and shut the door), and it is not a contradiction of election (God's patience is itself the means by which the elect are gathered). It is the breathtaking truth that the apparent delay of the parousia is not divine procrastination — it is divine love, actively gathering those who are His.

New creation as promise: The new heavens and new earth of verse 13 is the eschatological horizon of the entire epistle — and of the entire New Testament. Herman Bavinck's axiom — grace restores nature — finds its ultimate expression here: the fire does not destroy the creation but purifies it; the new creation is this creation glorified, the world God made very good and will make even better. Anthony Hoekema's The Bible and the Future demonstrates that the new earth is not a replacement but a renewal — which is why Christian hope is not escapism but engagement: the world we tend and serve and love matters eternally, because it is the world God intends to redeem.
3.examples:
Then: The scoffers' question — 'Where is the promise of his coming?' — has been asked in every generation. The first generation of believers died; the second, the third, the hundredth. Each generation has faced the apparent delay, and the temptation to conclude that the promise was empty. Peter's answer remains the same across every generation: God is not slow. He is patient. His patience is not weakness — it is mercy in motion, gathering those who are still to be gathered before the door closes. Every generation of Christians lives in the overlap of promise and fulfilment, patience and urgency.

Now: 'What sort of people ought you to be?' (v. 11) is the most searching pastoral question the letter asks, and it lands as heavily today as it did in the first century. The return of Christ has not yet come — but it is coming, and it is certain. The question is not about calculation but about formation. The person who genuinely believes the Day is coming will live differently: with moral seriousness, with urgency about the gospel, with detachment from the world's false securities, with eager longing for righteousness. The Christian who has domesticated eschatology into a theological opinion without ethical bite has not yet let 2 Peter 3 do its work. Let it. Grow in the grace and knowledge of our Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ. That is the whole assignment — and it will last exactly until the Day of eternity.
